about: The left-hand column of the Finds map: physical finds and a few ancient texts outside the Bible, in rough date order. Each link says how the find touches an event. Seeded 24 October 2026 by Barnabas from memory of standard reference works (Hoffmeier, Kitchen, Mykytiuk, the museum catalogues). Facts here are CONSENSUS unless a link is graded DISPUTED; reverify a detail before Kev teaches it.

linkTypes.names: Names a person the Bible names
linkTypes.confirms: Confirms an event, custom or detail of the text
linkTypes.setting: Shows the place or world the text describes was real
linkTypes.parallel: A parallel story or claimed link, not confirmation

finds.name: Enuma Elish tablets
finds.when: c. 1100 BC copies of an older text
finds.summary: The Babylonian creation epic. The god Marduk builds the world from the body of a defeated sea goddess. It is a parallel that sharpens the contrast with Genesis 1: one God, no rivals, creating by his word.

links.note: Shared ancient Near Eastern backdrop, very different theology.

finds.name: Gilgamesh Flood Tablet (Tablet XI)
finds.when: 7th century BC copy of an older story
finds.summary: Utnapishtim survives a great flood in a boat, sends out birds and offers a sacrifice. When George Smith read it in 1872 it caused a sensation for its closeness to Genesis 6-9.

links.note: A parallel memory of a flood; not physical evidence.

finds.name: Atrahasis Epic
finds.summary: An older Mesopotamian story that runs from the making of humans to a flood sent by the gods. Like Genesis 1-9, it moves from creation to flood in one sweep.

links.note: Creation-to-flood structure, as in Genesis.
A flood hero is warned and builds a boat.

finds.name: Sumerian King List (Weld-Blundell Prism)
finds.summary: Lists kings before the flood with enormous reigns, then a break: 'after the flood swept over'. It shows Mesopotamia remembered a dividing flood, and long lives before it, as in Genesis 5.

links.note: Kings before and after a flood.

finds.name: Ur: Royal Cemetery and ziggurat
finds.nowAt: Finds at the Penn Museum, the British Museum and the Iraq Museum
finds.summary: Leonard Woolley's dig (1922-34) showed Ur as a wealthy city with a great stepped temple tower. Genesis names it as Abram's starting point.

links.note: A real ziggurat of the kind Genesis 11 describes.
Ur was real and great (Genesis 11:31). Whether Abram's Ur is this southern city or a northern one is debated.

finds.name: Ebla tablets
finds.nowAt: Museums of Idlib and Aleppo, Syria
finds.summary: About 17,000 tablets and fragments from an early Syrian kingdom. Early claims that they named Sodom, Gomorrah and biblical figures were later withdrawn.

links.note: Early sensational readings did not hold up. Kept here only as a caution.

finds.name: Mari tablets
finds.nowAt: Louvre, and museums in Aleppo and Damascus
finds.summary: About 25,000 tablets from a royal archive. They name towns called Nahor and Haran in the region Genesis gives for Abraham's family, and describe tribal herders moving between towns.

links.note: Haran and Nahor as real places (Genesis 11:31; 24:10). Abraham is not named.

finds.name: Nuzi tablets
finds.nowAt: Harvard Semitic Museum and the Iraq Museum
finds.summary: Family law contracts once read as close matches for customs in Genesis, such as a servant bearing an heir for a childless wife.

links.note: Many early parallels were overstated. A few still hold.

finds.name: Beni Hasan tomb painting
finds.place: Tomb of Khnumhotep II, Middle Egypt
finds.summary: Shows a party of 37 Asiatics (Aamu) led by a chief called Abisha entering Egypt with goods, donkeys and colourful robes.

links.note: Semitic families traveling down into Egypt, as in Genesis 12 and 42-46.
Asiatics trading with and entering Egypt in the period.

finds.name: Tell el-Dab'a (Avaris)
finds.nowAt: Site; Austrian Archaeological Institute excavations under Manfred Bietak
finds.summary: A large town in the eastern Delta with Canaanite-style houses, burials and pottery. It is the land of Goshen region in Genesis 47.

links.note: A Semitic population settled in the Delta. Claims of 'Joseph's house' or tomb are speculation.

finds.name: Brooklyn Papyrus 35.1446
finds.summary: A list of 95 household servants in one Egyptian estate; more than 40 are Asiatics with Semitic names. One is a woman named Shiphrah, like the Hebrew midwife of Exodus 1:15.

links.note: Semites serving in Egyptian households, as Joseph did.
The same name, Shiphrah, not the same woman.

finds.name: Soleb temple inscription
finds.place: Temple of Amenhotep III, Soleb, Sudan
finds.summary: Lists 'the land of the Shasu of Yhw', a group of nomads south of Canaan. Many scholars read Yhw as the earliest outside mention of the divine name YHWH.

links.note: A place or people named Yhw. The link to Israel's God is likely but debated.

finds.name: Pi-Ramesses (Qantir)
finds.summary: The great Delta capital of Ramesses II, built with mud brick. Exodus 1:11 says Hebrew slaves built the store city Raamses.

links.note: The city named in Exodus 1:11 was real. What it says about the date of the Exodus is debated.

finds.name: Amarna letters
finds.nowAt: Berlin, British Museum, Cairo and others
finds.summary: About 380 clay letters to Pharaoh, many from kings of Canaanite cities. Abdi-Heba of Jerusalem pleads for troops against the Habiru, raiders who are troubling the land.

links.note: Canaan as a patchwork of city-kings, Jerusalem among them, as in Joshua 10.
Whether the Habiru include the Hebrews is debated; most say the term is a social class, not a people.

finds.name: Merneptah Stele
finds.summary: Pharaoh Merneptah boasts of a campaign in Canaan: 'Israel is laid waste, his seed is not.' The sign used marks Israel as a people, not a city. It is the oldest outside mention of Israel.

links.note: Israel was a known people in Canaan by about 1208 BC.

finds.name: Jericho (Tell es-Sultan)
finds.when: Destruction layers in the Bronze Age
finds.summary: Garstang dated a burnt city with fallen walls to about 1400 BC. Kenyon redated it to about 1550 BC. Bryant Wood argued again for 1400 BC.

links.note: The fallen walls and burn layer are real. Their date is argued.

finds.name: Hazor destruction layer
finds.summary: The largest Canaanite city was burned in a fierce fire. Joshua 11:13 says Hazor alone of the northern cities was burned.

links.note: Amnon Ben-Tor credits the Israelites. Others suggest Egyptians, Sea Peoples or civil revolt.

finds.name: Deir Alla inscription (Balaam text)
finds.summary: Ink on plaster, written about 'Balaam son of Beor, a seer of the gods' who receives a night vision. It is the same name and title as the prophet of Numbers 22-24.

links.note: Balaam son of Beor, remembered east of the Jordan centuries later.

finds.name: Tell es-Safi (Gath) and its ostracon
finds.summary: Gath was a large Philistine city, as 1 Samuel describes. A potsherd from about 950 BC has two non-Semitic names, ALWT and WLT, that are close to the form of the name Goliath.

links.note: Goliath's city was real and powerful (1 Samuel 17:4).
A name like Goliath's, not Goliath himself.

finds.name: Khirbet Qeiyafa
finds.nowAt: Site; ostracon in the Israel Museum
finds.summary: A fortified town with two gates overlooking the valley where David met Goliath. It produced a short early Hebrew or Canaanite ostracon.

links.note: Yosef Garfinkel sees a Judahite town of David's time. Others assign it to Philistines or Canaanites.

finds.name: Tel Dan Stele
finds.summary: An Aramean king, almost certainly Hazael, boasts of killing a king of Israel and a king of the 'House of David' (bytdwd). It is the first outside mention of David.

links.note: David as founder of Judah's royal house.
Wars between Aram and Israel (2 Kings 8-9). The stele credits Hazael with deaths that 2 Kings credits to Jehu.

finds.name: Mesha Stele (Moabite Stone)
finds.summary: King Mesha of Moab tells how 'Omri, king of Israel' oppressed Moab and how he rebelled. It names the God of Israel, YHWH, and may mention the 'House of David'.

links.note: Omri, and Moab's revolt against Israel (2 Kings 3:4-5).
Line 31 may read 'House of David' (André Lemaire). The text there is damaged.

finds.name: Gezer Calendar
finds.summary: A schoolboy-style list of the farming year: olive harvest, sowing, flax, barley, grapes, summer fruit. It is one of the oldest Hebrew-family inscriptions.

links.note: Writing and farm life in Solomon's century.

finds.name: Six-chambered gates at Gezer, Hazor, Megiddo
finds.summary: Yigael Yadin found matching gate plans at the three cities 1 Kings 9:15 says Solomon built.

links.note: Yadin, Dever and Mazar date them to Solomon. Israel Finkelstein's low chronology moves them later.

finds.name: Shishak (Shoshenq I) relief
finds.nowAt: In place; a stele fragment from Megiddo is in the Rockefeller Museum
finds.summary: Pharaoh Shoshenq I lists more than 150 towns he struck in Israel and Judah. 1 Kings 14:25 says Shishak came against Jerusalem in Rehoboam's fifth year.

links.note: Shishak's campaign just after Solomon (1 Kings 14:25-26).

finds.name: Kurkh Monolith
finds.summary: Shalmaneser III of Assyria lists his enemies at the battle of Qarqar, among them 'Ahab the Israelite' with 2,000 chariots.

links.note: Ahab as a major military power. The Bible does not record Qarqar.

finds.name: Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III
finds.summary: One panel shows 'Jehu son of Omri' (Omri's dynastic name) bowing before the Assyrian king with tribute. It is the only known image of a king of Israel or Judah.

links.note: Jehu, king of Israel (2 Kings 9-10).

finds.name: Samaria ivories
finds.nowAt: Israel Museum and the Rockefeller Museum
finds.summary: Hundreds of carved ivory inlays from the palace of Israel's kings. 1 Kings 22:39 speaks of Ahab's 'ivory house', and Amos condemns 'beds of ivory'.

links.note: Ivory luxury at Samaria (1 Kings 22:39; Amos 3:15; 6:4).

finds.name: Seal of Shema, servant of Jeroboam
finds.nowAt: Lost in Istanbul; a bronze cast survives
finds.summary: A jasper seal with a roaring lion, inscribed 'Belonging to Shema, servant of Jeroboam'.

links.note: Most date it to Jeroboam II (2 Kings 14:23). A few argue for Jeroboam I.

finds.name: Annals of Tiglath-pileser III
finds.summary: Name tribute from Menahem of Samaria, Ahaz (Jehoahaz) of Judah, the overthrow of Pekah, and the installing of Hoshea.

links.note: Menahem, Pekah, Hoshea and Ahaz (2 Kings 15-16). The Bible also calls this king Pul.

finds.name: Sargon II inscriptions, Khorsabad
finds.nowAt: Louvre and the Oriental Institute, Chicago
finds.summary: Sargon claims he deported 27,290 people from Samaria. Before Khorsabad was dug in 1843, Isaiah 20:1 was the only ancient text that named Sargon at all.

links.note: The fall and deportation of Samaria (2 Kings 17:6).
Sargon himself, named in Isaiah 20:1.

finds.name: Sennacherib Prism
finds.nowAt: British Museum (Taylor Prism), Oriental Institute Chicago, Israel Museum
finds.summary: Sennacherib says he took 46 walled cities of Judah and shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem 'like a bird in a cage'. He lists Hezekiah's tribute but never claims to have taken the city.

links.note: Hezekiah of Judah by name.
The siege and the tribute (2 Kings 18:13-16). Jerusalem was not taken (2 Kings 19:32-36).

finds.name: Lachish reliefs
finds.summary: A wall-length carving of the Assyrian assault on Lachish: siege ramps, archers and captives led away. The siege ramp is still visible at Tel Lachish.

links.note: Sennacherib at Lachish (2 Kings 18:14, 17).

finds.name: Hezekiah's Tunnel and the Siloam Inscription
finds.nowAt: Tunnel in place; inscription in the Istanbul Archaeology Museums
finds.summary: A 533-metre tunnel cut through rock from the Gihon Spring. The inscription tells how two crews of diggers met in the middle.

links.note: Hezekiah brought water into the city (2 Kings 20:20; 2 Chronicles 32:30).

finds.name: Royal bulla of Hezekiah
finds.summary: A clay seal impression: 'Belonging to Hezekiah [son of] Ahaz, king of Judah', with a winged sun. Found in a controlled dig, not bought on the market.

links.note: Hezekiah and his father Ahaz (2 Kings 18:1).

finds.name: Possible Isaiah bulla
finds.summary: Found about 3 metres from the Hezekiah bulla. It reads 'Yesha'yah[u]' and then letters that may be the start of 'prophet'. The edge is broken.

links.note: The missing letter decides whether it says 'prophet'.

finds.name: The Broad Wall
finds.summary: A 7-metre-thick wall built across the remains of houses, as the city expanded west before the Assyrian threat.

links.note: Isaiah 22:10 says houses were torn down to fortify the wall.

finds.name: LMLK royal jar handles
finds.summary: Thousands of jar handles stamped 'belonging to the king' with a place name, from Judah's royal supply system.

links.note: Royal storehouses for grain, wine and oil (2 Chronicles 32:27-29).

finds.name: Ketef Hinnom silver scrolls
finds.summary: Two tiny rolled silver amulets carry the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24-26. They are the oldest known copies of any text of Scripture.

links.note: The blessing was in use, in this form, before the exile.
Faith in YHWH in Jerusalem in Jeremiah's day.

finds.name: Bulla of Gemariah son of Shaphan
finds.place: City of David, Jerusalem (Yigal Shiloh's dig, 1982)
finds.summary: One of 51 seal impressions found in a burned archive room. It names Gemariah son of Shaphan, in whose chamber Baruch read Jeremiah's scroll.

links.note: Jeremiah 36:10-12.

finds.name: Bullae of Jehucal and Gedaliah
finds.summary: Two seal impressions found metres apart: 'Jehucal son of Shelemiah' and 'Gedaliah son of Pashhur'. Jeremiah 38:1 names both men together as the officials who wanted Jeremiah dead.

links.note: Jeremiah 38:1.

finds.name: Bulla of Nathan-melech
finds.place: City of David, Givati parking lot (2019)
finds.summary: 'Belonging to Nathan-melech, servant of the king'. 2 Kings 23:11 names a Nathan-melech, an official in Josiah's court.

links.note: Probably the same official (2 Kings 23:11). The name is rare.

finds.name: Lachish Letters
finds.nowAt: British Museum and the Israel Museum
finds.summary: Ink letters on pottery from an outpost commander as Babylon closed in. Letter 4: they watch for Lachish's fire signals 'for we cannot see Azekah'.

links.note: Jeremiah 34:7: only Lachish and Azekah were left of Judah's fortified cities.

finds.name: Babylonian Chronicle (BM 21946)
finds.summary: Records that Nebuchadnezzar besieged 'the city of Judah', took it on 2 Adar (16 March 597 BC), seized its king and appointed a king of his own choice.

links.note: 2 Kings 24:10-17, to the day.

finds.name: Jehoiachin ration tablets
finds.summary: Palace records of oil rations for 'Ya'ukin, king of the land of Yahud' and his five sons.

links.note: Jehoiachin, a captive king at Babylon's table (2 Kings 25:27-30).

finds.name: Nebo-Sarsekim tablet
finds.summary: A receipt for gold paid by 'Nabu-sharrussu-ukin, the chief eunuch' of Nebuchadnezzar. Jeremiah 39:3 names a Babylonian official Sarsechim at the fall of Jerusalem.

links.note: Widely accepted as the same official. Some debate how to split the names in Jeremiah 39:3.

finds.name: Ishtar Gate and Nebuchadnezzar's bricks
finds.summary: Blue glazed brick with lions and dragons. Thousands of bricks are stamped with Nebuchadnezzar's name, and he boasts of building Babylon.

links.note: Nebuchadnezzar and his building pride (Daniel 4:30).

finds.name: Nabonidus Cylinder and Chronicle
finds.summary: Nabonidus prays for 'Belshazzar, my eldest son'. The Chronicle shows Nabonidus away at Tema for years while his son ruled in Babylon. Before these were read, critics said Belshazzar never existed.

links.note: Belshazzar as acting king. It explains why he offers Daniel 'third ruler' (Daniel 5:16). When Daniel was written is a separate debate.

finds.name: Al-Yahudu tablets
finds.nowAt: Private collections; shown at the Bible Lands Museum, Jerusalem
finds.summary: About 200 business records from 'Al-Yahudu', meaning 'the town of Judah', a village of Judean exiles. Many names carry Yahweh, like Yahu-azar.

links.note: Judean exiles settled in towns of their own (Jeremiah 29:4-7; Ezekiel 3:15).

finds.name: Cyrus Cylinder
finds.summary: Cyrus records that he returned captive peoples and their gods to their homelands and rebuilt their shrines.

links.note: The policy behind Ezra 1:1-4. It names Mesopotamian cities, not Judah.

finds.name: Susa palace of Darius and Xerxes
finds.summary: The French dig found the royal palace, its gate and its court. The layout fits the setting of Esther, and Persian texts confirm Ahasuerus as Xerxes I.

links.note: Esther 1:2 and the king's gate (Esther 2:19). Mordecai and Esther are not named in any find.

finds.name: Elephantine papyri
finds.nowAt: Brooklyn Museum and the Berlin collections
finds.summary: A Jewish garrison in Egypt writes to Persia's governor of Judah. Their letters name Sanballat governor of Samaria and Johanan the high priest.

links.note: Sanballat (Nehemiah 2:10) and Johanan (Nehemiah 12:22).

finds.name: Dead Sea Scrolls and the Great Isaiah Scroll
finds.when: c. 250 BC-AD 68; Isaiah scroll c. 125 BC
finds.nowAt: Shrine of the Book, Israel Museum, Jerusalem
finds.summary: Fragments of every Old Testament book except Esther. The complete Isaiah scroll is about 1,000 years older than the earlier oldest Hebrew copies, and it agrees closely with them.

links.note: The text Jesus read (Luke 4:17) was copied faithfully. The differences are mostly spelling.

finds.name: Herodium and Herod's tomb
finds.nowAt: Site; sarcophagus at the Israel Museum
finds.summary: Herod the Great's fortress palace, in sight of Bethlehem. Ehud Netzer found his tomb on its slope after a 35-year search.

links.note: Herod the king (Matthew 2:1), ruling from Bethlehem's horizon.

finds.name: Lapis Venetus (Quirinius census inscription)
finds.summary: A Roman officer says he carried out a census of the city of Apamea on the orders of Quirinius, governor of Syria.

links.note: Quirinius and his census are real (Luke 2:2). How it fits with Herod's death in 4 BC is a long-running debate, with several proposals.

finds.name: First-century house at Nazareth
finds.summary: A courtyard house cut partly into the hillside, studied by Ken Dark. It showed that Nazareth was a small Jewish village in Jesus' day, against claims it did not exist.

links.note: Nazareth existed in Jesus' time (Luke 4:16). Whose house it was is unknown.

finds.name: Magdala synagogue and stone
finds.nowAt: Site; the stone is a replica in place
finds.summary: A first-century synagogue in Mary Magdalene's town. A carved stone in it shows a seven-branched menorah.

links.note: Jesus taught in the synagogues of Galilee (Matthew 4:23; Luke 8:2).

finds.name: Galilee Boat (Ginosar)
finds.summary: An 8-metre fishing boat from the time of Jesus, room for about a dozen people, preserved in the mud.

links.note: The kind of boat the disciples fished from (Mark 4:35-41). There is no reason to tie it to them.

finds.name: Capernaum synagogue foundation
finds.summary: Under the white limestone synagogue of the 4th century lie black basalt walls that many date to the first century.

links.note: Likely the synagogue where Jesus taught (Mark 1:21). Its first-century date is argued.

finds.name: Pool of Bethesda
finds.summary: Excavations found two large pools with porticoes around and between them. Critics once called John's 'five roofed colonnades' made up.

links.note: John 5:2, down to the colonnades.

finds.name: Pool of Siloam (Second Temple)
finds.summary: Sewer workers found steps of a large stepped pool from Jesus' day, at the end of the water system Hezekiah cut.

links.note: 'Go, wash in the pool of Siloam' (John 9:7).

finds.name: Pilate Stone
finds.summary: A building dedication reading '[Pon]tius Pilatus, [Praef]ectus Iuda[ea]e'. It is the only inscription from his lifetime that names him, and it gives his exact title.

links.note: Pontius Pilate, governor of Judea (Mark 15:1).

finds.name: Caiaphas ossuary
finds.summary: An ornate bone box inscribed 'Yehosef bar Qayafa', Joseph son of Caiaphas. Josephus gives the high priest's full name as Joseph Caiaphas.

links.note: Most accept it as the high priest's family tomb (Matthew 26:57). Some question the reading and the link.

finds.name: Heel bone of Yehohanan
finds.summary: A heel bone still pierced by an iron nail, from a young man crucified and then buried in a family tomb.

links.note: How Rome crucified, and that a crucified man could get a proper burial, as Joseph of Arimathea gave Jesus (Mark 15:43-46).

finds.name: Tacitus, Annals 15.44
finds.summary: A hostile Roman historian: 'Christus' was executed under Tiberius by the procurator Pontius Pilate, and his followers were blamed for the fire of Rome.

links.note: The execution under Pilate, from outside the church.

finds.name: Josephus, Antiquities 18 and 20
finds.summary: Josephus mentions 'James, the brother of Jesus who was called Christ', stoned in AD 62. A longer passage about Jesus (18.63-64) was later expanded by Christian copyists.

links.note: Antiquities 20.200 on James and Jesus is accepted as genuine.
The Testimonium (18.63-64): most scholars hold that a genuine core was later expanded.
James, leader in Jerusalem (Acts 15:13; Galatians 1:19).

finds.name: Temple warning inscription
finds.nowAt: Istanbul Archaeology Museums; a fragment in the Israel Museum
finds.summary: A Greek notice from the barrier around the inner courts: any foreigner who goes past it has himself to blame for his death that follows.

links.note: The riot when Paul was said to bring Greeks into the temple (Acts 21:28-29); 'the dividing wall of hostility' (Ephesians 2:14).

finds.name: Theodotus inscription
finds.summary: Theodotus, priest and synagogue leader, built a synagogue for reading the Law and a guest house for visitors from abroad.

links.note: Synagogues in Jerusalem for Greek-speaking Jews (Acts 6:9). The pre-70 date is accepted by most.

finds.name: Sergius Paullus inscriptions
finds.nowAt: Museums in Rome and Yalvaç, Turkey
finds.summary: Inscriptions name members of the Sergius Paullus family. One lists a Lucius Sergius Paullus among Rome's officials for the Tiber.

links.note: Possibly the proconsul of Cyprus who believed (Acts 13:7-12). The link is not certain.

finds.name: Politarch inscription, Vardar Gate
finds.summary: Lists the city's 'politarchs'. Critics once said Luke invented this title. More than 30 inscriptions now use it, most of them from Macedonia.

links.note: The 'city authorities' of Thessalonica (Acts 17:6, 8).

finds.name: Gallio Inscription (Delphi)
finds.summary: A letter from Emperor Claudius names 'Junius Gallio, my friend, the proconsul' of Achaia. It fixes Gallio's term to about AD 51-52.

links.note: Gallio (Acts 18:12). This is the anchor for dating Paul's journeys.

finds.name: Erastus inscription (Corinth)
finds.summary: 'Erastus, in return for his aedileship, laid [this pavement] at his own expense.' Paul sends greetings from 'Erastus, the city treasurer' in Romans 16:23.

links.note: Possibly Paul's Erastus. The inscription's date and the match of offices are debated.

finds.name: Ephesus theatre and the Artemis cult
finds.summary: A theatre seating about 25,000, and inscriptions about the cult of Artemis, its silversmiths, and the city's title 'temple keeper'.

links.note: The riot of the silversmiths in the theatre (Acts 19:23-41), with the city clerk and 'temple keeper' (19:35).

finds.name: Arch of Titus
finds.summary: A triumphal arch carved with Roman soldiers carrying the temple's lampstand, trumpets and table of showbread out of Jerusalem.

links.note: The temple's fall that Jesus foretold (Luke 21:6).

finds.name: Burnt House and the fallen temple stones
finds.place: Jewish Quarter and Robinson's Arch, Jerusalem
finds.summary: A priestly family's house (Kathros) burned in AD 70, with a spear and a young woman's arm bones. Below the Temple Mount, huge stones lie where Rome pushed them onto the street.

links.note: 'Not one stone here will be left on another' (Matthew 24:2).

finds.name: Laodicea's water pipes
finds.summary: Laodicea piped its water from springs miles away. The terracotta pipes are thick with mineral crust. Nearby Hierapolis had hot springs and Colossae had cold water.

links.note: Many read 'neither hot nor cold' (Revelation 3:15-16) against this. That is an interpretation, though the setting is real.

finds.name: Pergamum Altar of Zeus
finds.summary: A colossal altar on the acropolis. Pergamum was also a center of the imperial cult and of the healing god Asclepius.

links.note: One of several candidates for 'where Satan's throne is' (Revelation 2:13).

finds.name: Temple of the Sebastoi, Ephesus
finds.nowAt: Site; colossal statue head in the Ephesus Museum, Selçuk
finds.summary: A temple to the Flavian emperors with a colossal cult statue, dedicated in Domitian's reign.

links.note: Emperor worship in Asia, the pressure behind Revelation 13 and the letters to the churches.

leftOff.name: James ossuary
leftOff.why: The box is ancient. Whether the words 'brother of Jesus' were added later is still argued. A forgery trial ended in 2012 without settling it.

leftOff.name: Museum of the Bible Dead Sea Scroll fragments
leftOff.why: Shown in 2018 and 2020 to be modern forgeries.

leftOff.name: Noah's Ark sightings and 'chariot wheels' in the Red Sea
leftOff.why: No verified evidence. Repeating them harms the credibility of real finds.

leftOff.name: The 'Jesus Family Tomb' (Talpiot)
leftOff.why: Common names. Rejected by most archaeologists.
